On this page

Plans & Tasks ​

A Run's plan is a checklist of tasks with contracts attached. The contract is written before the work starts, which is the only moment at which it can be honest.

A task ​

ts
interface ChecklistItem {
  id?: string;
  text: string;
  status?: 'pending' | 'running' | 'blocked' | 'done' | 'failed';
  assignee?: string;            // project or agent responsible
  dependsOn?: string[];         // other task ids that must finish first
  mode?: 'ask' | 'work';
  effort?: EffortMode;          // spend deliberately, per task
  acceptanceCriteria?: string[];
  checks?: TaskCheck[];         // shell commands judged by exit code
  proofs?: TaskProof[];         // fileExists / assetCount
  evidence?: string;            // what the DOER reported — not proof
  verification?: TaskVerification;  // the independent verdict
  attemptBudget?: number;
}

Observable criteria ​

A criterion has to be something a verifier could rule on. The engine checks this at plan time.

Observable ✓Not observable ✗
`npm run build` succeeds with no errorsthe copy is good
dist/report.pdf existslooks professional
the endpoint returns 200high quality writing
the page lists three tierswell structured
a summary file is created in output/the user will be happy

Criteria are required on new plans (set_plan / amend_plan).

Checks: mechanical proof ​

A TaskCheck is a shell command whose exit code decides. It runs in the run's own workspace with a sanitized env and a short timeout, and it is always shown to the doer in its brief — a check the agent cannot see is a trap, not a contract.

ts
{ cmd: 'npm test', expectExit: 0, criterion: 'the suite passes' }

The trust asymmetry ​

A check may be trusted only if it came from a source the run did not author — project config, or an operator. This is not bureaucracy:

  • A failing check is real evidence of failure no matter who wrote it. So any check can fail a task.
  • A passing check is only as trustworthy as its author — and the plan author writes both the criteria and the checks. {cmd: "true", criterion: "<copy of a real criterion>"} passes plan validation and certifies the task.

So an untrusted check can only ever make the gate stricter, never weaker. trusted is not settable from the plan schema: nothing a model writes is trusted by construction.

Proofs: a closed vocabulary ​

Where a shell command is too much rope, a TaskProof is engine-evaluable and read-only:

kindProves
fileExistsA path exists, relative to the workspace (no glob suffix matching, deliberately)
assetCountAt least minCount run assets exist, optionally of a given extension

Because the vocabulary is closed, a proof may safely certify the criterion it names.

Task state flow ​

ChecklistItem.status is pending | running | blocked | done | failed.

Verification ​

ts
interface TaskVerification {
  status: 'passed' | 'failed' | 'skipped';
  by: 'command' | 'evidence' | 'model' | 'none';
  reason?: string;
  failureKind?: 'work_missing' | 'semantic_failure' | 'proof_missing'
              | 'environment_failure' | 'provider_failure';
  at: number;
}

A task may only reach done on a passed (or explicitly skipped) verification. failureKind exists so a retry can be routed — an environment failure and a semantic failure do not deserve the same response, and treating every rejection as "redo the whole task" burns budget.

Verdicts also append to the run-level verificationLog, which survives plan amendments that drop the task. One real run amended twice, discarding three rejections of the task it gave up on, and the run's record then showed three verdicts where six had happened.

Evidence ​

The engine collects evidence itself rather than trusting the report:

  • EvidenceCommand — cmd, exit code, duration, output tail.
  • EvidenceArtifact — path, kind, size, sha256.
  • EvidenceChanges — read straight off git: the branch, its nearest-ancestor base, the commits, and per-file additions/deletions. Free to collect, and it needs nothing from the plan author, who writes the contract before the artifacts exist.

Drift ​

originalChecklist keeps the plan exactly as first frozen. planVersion starts at 1 and is bumped by every accepted amendment — a repeatable run should still read 1 at the end. The engine also tracks unverified done tasks: anything marked complete that no gate ever ruled on.

Plan approval ​

planApproval is operator sign-off on the plan, not the work. Guarding the contract before any task runs answers "is this the right work"; verification answers the separate question "was the work actually done".

Playbooks ​

When a run's plan is replayed from a saved playbook rather than re-derived, playbookId records it. Same brief → same plan is the strongest form of repeatability Saidi offers.
